acts.title: The office with the slide in it
text: We have all seen photographs of striking, ___ offices with slides and ping-pong tables.
Free food and free dry-cleaning are real ___, and nobody who has them wants to give them up.
What the research keeps finding, though, is that the loudest offices are the most ___ .

acts.title: Text A · What actually helps you think
text: Most people have a theory about how they work best, and most of those theories turn out to be wrong.

Silence is the first casualty. According to research by Professor Ravi Mehta, a moderate level of noise is better for creative work than quiet. Too much is still bad, and one kind is worse than any other: overhearing half a phone call, because the brain keeps trying to solve the missing side.
Temperature is the second. One Cornell study found that at twenty degrees employees made forty-four per cent more mistakes than at twenty-five. If you are cold, you are spending energy on being warm.
The third is the desk. Having a messy desk turns out to be better for inventiveness than having it tidied, which is a sentence I have had framed.
And the fourth is tiredness. A tired brain is less efficient and more likely to make new connections, which is not the same thing as being useless.

items.q: What is the main finding of Text A?
o: Most people’s assumptions about working conditions are wrong

items.q: Which kind of noise does the text say is worst?
o: Hearing one half of a phone conversation

acts.title: Text B · The bus that had a jumper made for it
text: A lamp post you have walked past for years is suddenly multicoloured. Trees, statues, even buses find themselves wearing a knitted cover. It is called yarn-bombing.

It is believed to have started in the United States and is now global. In Paris a yarn-bomber has had the cracks in the pavement filled with wool. In Poland, Agata Oleksiak covered her grandmother’s house with a loose knitted cover. In Mexico City, Magda Sayeg had a perfectly fitting cover made for a city bus.

It is a kind of street art, a little like graffiti but far less damaging, because it can simply be removed. Many local governments dislike it anyway, so it is usually done at night. Knitting is very quiet.

The larger artists do not work alone. Both Oleksiak and Sayeg have teams of people help them, and they get the results photographed and posted online. The stated aim is small: to make an ugly object better and to put a smile on somebody’s face.

items.s: Yarn-bombing is thought to have begun in the United States.
It is more damaging than graffiti.
It is usually done at night because many councils dislike it.
The best-known yarn-bombers work entirely alone.
The results are photographed and posted online.

items.q: What is the order in have something done?

acts.title: Getting somebody else to do it
rule: The causative says that you arranged for something rather than doing it. English keeps the two ideas apart with word order alone, which is why the structure is easy to understand and hard to produce: the object goes in the middle, and the participle comes after it.
points: have + object + past participle. I had the car repaired. Neutral, and the standard written choice.
Identical in meaning, more informal, and often used when there was some effort involved.
have + person + bare infinitive. I had the mechanic look at it. You are naming who.
get + person + to + infinitive. Slightly more persuasion implied.
have something done can also mean something unpleasant happened to you: I had my phone stolen. Nobody arranged that.
eg: I had the car repaired last week.
Arranged; a garage did it.
I’m getting the roof fixed on Tuesday.
Same meaning, informal.
She had a cover made for a city bus.
She arranged it; somebody else knitted it.
I had the mechanic look at it.
Naming the person: bare infinitive.
I got my brother to look at it.
get + person + to + infinitive.
We had the whole flat redecorated.
The commonest textbook example, and genuinely common.
They get the results photographed and posted online.
Two participles sharing one get.
I had my phone stolen on the underground.
Nobody arranged this — the bad-news use.
You should have that tooth looked at.
With a modal.
Where do you have your hair cut?
Question form — the object still sits in the middle.
acts.careful: “I had repaired the car” means you repaired it yourself, in the past perfect. “I had the car repaired” means a garage did it. The only difference is where the object sits.

acts.title: From who did it to who arranged it
steps: Start with who actually did the work.
1 · The person who ARRANGED it becomes the subject.
2 · The thing goes next. This is the step learners skip.
I had the car repaired at the garage on Bukhar Zhyrau.
4 · Add where or by whom only if it matters.

items.from: A garage repaired my car last week.

steps.cue: Rewrite it with HAVE SOMETHING DONE
steps.a: I had the car repaired last week
steps.why: The object goes between have and the participle. That word order is the whole structure.

steps.cue: Now say it informally, with GET
steps.a: I got the car repaired last week

items.from: Somebody will take the photographs on Friday.

steps.cue: Rewrite it with WILL HAVE and a participle
steps.a: We will have the photographs taken on Friday
alt: We’ll have the photographs taken on Friday

steps.cue: Now name the person doing it: a photographer
steps.a: We will have a photographer take them
alt: We’ll have a photographer take them
steps.why: When you name the person, the next word is a bare infinitive: have somebody do.

items.from: Somebody stole my phone on the underground.

steps.cue: Rewrite it with HAD, so that it happened TO you
steps.a: I had my phone stolen on the underground

steps.cue: Now say what you need to arrange next, with NEED TO HAVE
steps.a: I need to have it replaced

items.from: They photograph the results and post them online.

steps.cue: Rewrite it with GET and two participles
steps.a: They get the results photographed and posted online

steps.cue: Now put the whole thing in the plain PASSIVE instead
steps.a: The results are photographed and posted online
steps.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 25. The passive says it was done; the causative says somebody arranged it.

write.q: Write about 180 words on a place you spend time in — a flat, an office, a workshop — describing what you have had done to it, what you are getting done, and what still needs doing. Use have or get something done at least four times, and have or get somebody do something at least once. Include one example of the bad-news use.
plan: what you are getting done now
write.model:
The flat I live in was built in 1981 and looks it, but only in the places nobody visits.

In the first year I had the windows replaced, which cost more than everything else put together and was the only decision I have not regretted. I also had a friend of my father’s rewire the kitchen, because the previous arrangement had been done by somebody with strong opinions and no training.

At the moment I am getting the bathroom retiled, badly and slowly, by a man who answers his phone about one time in four.

What still needs doing is the balcony. I had the railing looked at two years ago and was told it was fine; I would now like to have it looked at by somebody who is not the person who installed it.

The low point was the winter I had my bicycle stolen from the stairwell, which is when I finally had a lock fitted on the outer door.
